heuristics.rule: A top-10 program with a poor advisor match produces worse outcomes than a top-30 program with an excellent advisor match
heuristics.condition: When choosing between a higher-ranked program with weak faculty fit and a lower-ranked program with strong advisor alignment
heuristics.action: Prioritize advisor match and research fit over program rank
heuristics.because: PhD outcomes are advisor-specific, not institution-specific — the advisor's placement record, funding, and mentorship quality drive actual career results

heuristics.rule: Never join a lab whose advisor has no active grants
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a PhD offer where the advisor's current grant status is unknown or inactive
heuristics.action: Verify active grants before accepting — if none exist, treat the offer as high-risk
heuristics.because: No active grants means no RA funding, no research budget, and likely no graduation support — the stipend offer may disappear mid-program

heuristics.rule: If you're qualified for a funded PhD, paying for an unfunded MS is a dominated choice
heuristics.condition: When an international student is deciding between a self-funded professional MS and a funded PhD program
heuristics.action: Apply for the funded PhD instead — it costs less, produces a stronger credential, and provides better immigration pathways
heuristics.because: An unfunded 2-year MS costs $150,000–$200,000 total; a funded PhD pays a stipend, waives tuition, and restarts OPT — better financial and career outcome in most cases

heuristics.rule: For academic job market targets, program prestige in your specific subfield matters more than overall ranking
heuristics.condition: When a student is targeting a tenure-track position and comparing programs
heuristics.action: Research subfield-specific reputation and hiring committee filtering practices, not just overall US News rank
heuristics.because: Hiring committees at research universities filter by program pedigree in first-round cuts — but subfield standing matters more than composite institutional rank

heuristics.rule: An advisor with 15+ PhD students cannot provide adequate mentorship to any individual student
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a potential advisor who has a very large current lab
heuristics.action: Treat high advisor-to-student ratio as a negative signal and investigate mentorship quality directly with current students
heuristics.because: Mentorship is finite — advising attention diluted across 15 students means less feedback, slower progress, and weaker career support per student

heuristics.rule: Check actual alumni placement outcomes before trusting prestige assumptions
heuristics.condition: When a student is optimizing for industry careers but considering a high-ranked program known for academic placements
heuristics.action: Ask the department where the last 5–10 cohorts actually went — not what the rank implies
heuristics.because: A top-5 program whose graduates mostly go into academia is a poor choice for industry-bound students regardless of prestige

heuristics.rule: Program location creates structural career advantages that rankings don't capture
heuristics.condition: When comparing otherwise similar programs in different geographies, especially for international students on OPT
heuristics.action: Favor programs in tech hubs or major metro areas if US industry employment is the goal
heuristics.because: OPT has a hard job-search deadline — Bay Area or NYC proximity provides denser recruiting pipelines, networking events, and internship access that structurally improve job search outcomes

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The single most predictive variable for academic career outcomes — more predictive than program rank because it reflects actual mentorship quality and professional network
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the advisor directly where their former PhD students are now; cross-reference on LinkedIn; ask current students about post-graduation support

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether the PhD is financially viable for an international student and whether the stipend will persist through the full program
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask whether stipend is guaranteed for 4–5 years regardless of advisor grant status, or year-by-year contingent on grants; verify advisor's active NSF/NIH/other grants

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Directly controls RA funding availability, research budget, and advisor's capacity to support the student through graduation
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Search NIH Reporter, NSF Award Search, or ask the advisor directly about active funded projects; look for recent grant renewals

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Average completion in 4 years vs. 7 years is a massive difference in opportunity cost, earning years, and immigration timeline
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the department directly for median time-to-degree data; ask current students how long peers typically take

decision_factors.factor: Program location relative to target job market
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Proximity to employer hubs creates structural recruiting advantages — especially critical for international students with OPT deadlines
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Map program location against target employer geography; ask alumni about recruiting pipeline access and internship frequency

decision_factors.factor: Alumni network strength in target industry or geography
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Strong alumni networks actively help graduates find jobs; weak networks leave students to self-navigate a cold market
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the department where alumni are; search LinkedIn for program alumni in your target role or geography; ask current students if alumni are responsive

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Matters specifically for academic hiring pipelines, elite consulting/finance recruiting, and home-country brand recognition — not for most industry careers
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify whether your specific career target (academic vs. industry vs. home country) is one where rank is a real screening filter

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines how much individual mentorship attention you will actually receive during the PhD
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Count current PhD students in the advisor's lab; ask current students how often they meet with the advisor one-on-one

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Collegial, collaborative departments produce better student outcomes and more tolerable multi-year experiences; toxic cultures cause attrition and mental health costs
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Visit if possible; observe seminar attendance and faculty-student interaction; speak privately with current PhD students without the advisor present

decision_factors.factor: Cost of living relative to stipend
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The same dollar stipend produces dramatically different quality of life and savings depending on location — affects financial stress over 5–6 years
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Compare stipend amount against city cost-of-living index; ask current students whether they can live comfortably on the stipend

decision_factors.why_it_matters: International students face unique bureaucratic, linguistic, and cultural challenges — strong ISSS and ESL resources reduce friction and risk
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check university ISSS website quality and responsiveness; ask international students about visa support experiences; assess community diversity in the department

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Academic hiring is subfield-specific — a department ranked 20th overall but 5th in your subfield may yield better academic outcomes than the reverse
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Look at subfield-specific rankings (e.g., CSRankings.org for CS, PGR for philosophy); check where subfield faculty publish and are cited

decision_factors.factor: MS vs. PhD structural funding difference
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The difference between a funded PhD and an unfunded MS can be $150,000–$200,000 in total cost — the largest financial variable in the decision
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify whether each program offers tuition waiver plus stipend or is tuition-paying; calculate total 2-year MS cost vs. 5-year PhD net income

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a PhD offer from a top-ranked program with an unfunded or under-funded advisor
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Stipend may disappear mid-program if advisor loses grant funding; student may be forced to TA indefinitely, slowing research progress and extending time-to-degree
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who cannot easily work outside their program and have no financial safety net

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Paying for a professional MS at a top-brand institution
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Total investment of $150,000–$200,000 with no guarantee of employment; international students cannot access US federal aid; OPT job search is time-pressured and may not recoup costs
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who are actually qualified for funded PhD programs but default to MS due to unfamiliarity with PhD funding structures

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a high-ranked program primarily for prestige with poor advisor fit
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Advisor relationship quality determines graduation support, reference letters, and network access — a prestigious program with a disengaged advisor leaves the student effectively unmentored and poorly positioned
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students targeting academic careers who rely on advisor-mediated hiring networks

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Attending a program in a low-cost-of-living university town for a higher stipend-to-cost ratio
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Structural disadvantage in recruiting — fewer internship opportunities, fewer employer recruiting events, harder OPT job search with hard deadlines
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students planning to work in US tech or finance industry post-graduation

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a lab with a very productive, highly cited advisor who has many PhD students
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Mentorship attention is diluted — students in large labs often receive less direct feedback, take longer to graduate, and compete internally for first-author opportunities
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who need active mentorship and frequent feedback to develop research independence

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Optimizing application strategy purely for top-10 programs without safety options
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Zero admission outcomes — a student rejected from all top-10 programs with no mid-tier or safety applications has no path forward for that cycle
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students with strong but not exceptional profiles who over-estimate their competitiveness at elite programs

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Selecting a program based on overall institutional ranking rather than alumni placement in your specific career track
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A highly ranked program whose alumni predominantly enter academia provides little industry network value; the prestige does not transfer to industry recruiting pipelines that aren't actively cultivated
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Industry-bound PhD students who assume prestige automatically converts to industry opportunity

failure_patterns.pattern: Applying only to top-10 prestige programs without considering faculty fit or building a tiered application list
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Rankings are the most visible and legible signal; students optimize for the most salient metric rather than the most predictive one
failure_patterns.consequence: Zero admissions in the application cycle; wasted application fees and a full year delay
warning_signs: Application list consists entirely of top-10 programs with no mid-tier or safety schools
Student cannot name specific faculty at target schools whose work directly aligns with their research interest

failure_patterns.pattern: Ignoring the advisor's current grant funding status before accepting a PhD offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students focus on the offer letter and stipend number without investigating whether the funding source is secure and multi-year
failure_patterns.consequence: Stipend evaporates mid-program; student is forced into TA roles that delay research; may not graduate on time or at all
warning_signs: Advisor cannot name a specific active grant when asked directly
Offer letter stipend is described as 'subject to funding availability' rather than guaranteed for a defined period

failure_patterns.pattern: Paying $150,000+ for an unfunded professional MS when a funded PhD was achievable
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: International students are often unfamiliar with US PhD funding norms and default to the MS track as the 'safer' or 'faster' path without calculating actual costs
failure_patterns.consequence: Massive debt or family financial burden; pressure to accept any job offer during OPT to recoup costs; worse career positioning than a funded PhD would have produced
warning_signs: Student has a strong research background and publications but is only applying to MS programs
Student has not explored whether PhD programs in their field offer full funding

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a PhD offer without visiting or interviewing current students and the advisor
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Excitement about acceptance, cost/logistics of visiting, or assumption that program quality is captured by ranking — students treat acceptance as sufficient information
failure_patterns.consequence: Discovering after enrollment that the advisor is unavailable, the lab culture is toxic, or the research direction mismatches expectations — at which point switching is costly
warning_signs: Student has never spoken directly with current PhD students in the lab
Student has not asked the advisor about mentorship style, meeting frequency, or current lab projects

failure_patterns.pattern: Optimizing for program ranking when your actual career target is industry, not academia
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Rankings create the illusion of universal quality signal; students conflate 'best program' with 'best program for my specific career goal'
failure_patterns.consequence: Graduates from highly ranked but industry-disconnected programs struggle in job searches that peers from lower-ranked but industry-connected programs navigate easily
warning_signs: Student cannot name the program's industry placement rate or alumni in their target role
Student assumes prestige automatically translates to recruiter interest without verifying employer recruiting patterns

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your intended career outcome — academic research, US industry, or returning to your home country?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines which decision variables (ranking, advisor network, location, brand recognition) are actually relevant to this person's situation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If academic: Which specific subfield, and have you identified faculty whose active research directly overlaps with your interest?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If industry or home country: Have you checked actual alumni placement data in that sector, not just assumed prestige transfers?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you verified the funding status of any PhD offer you've received — specifically whether the stipend is guaranteed for multiple years or contingent on the advisor's grant renewals?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the student understands the difference between a secure multi-year funding commitment and a precarious year-to-year offer
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If guaranteed: Is the guarantee at the department level or advisor level, and what happens if you switch advisors?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If not verified: Treat this as urgent — contact the department and ask directly before accepting

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you considering paying for an unfunded MS? If so, have you evaluated whether a funded PhD in the same field is achievable given your profile?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies whether the student is making a $150,000+ financial decision without exploring the funded alternative
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If PhD is achievable: What is the specific barrier preventing you from applying to funded PhD programs — timeline, research experience, or something else?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If PhD is not achievable: What is the employment outcome data for the specific MS program you're considering, and what is your plan during OPT?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you spoken directly with current PhD students in your target advisor's lab — without the advisor present?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the student has access to ground-truth information about advisor mentorship quality, lab culture, and time-to-degree
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: What did current students say about meeting frequency, feedback quality, and graduation support?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: This is the highest-value information-gathering action available before accepting — prioritize it

diagnostic_questions.question: Where is the program located, and how does that geography align with your target employers during OPT?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Surfaces whether the student has considered the structural recruiting advantage or disadvantage of program location under OPT time pressure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If aligned: Have you confirmed that recruiters from your target companies actively recruit at or near this program?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If misaligned: Do you have a plan to access recruiting networks remotely, or will you relocate during OPT?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the average time-to-degree for PhD students in this specific department, and where have graduates from the last 5 cohorts gone?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the student is evaluating actual outcomes versus assumed prestige, and whether the program produces graduates on a viable timeline
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If data is available: Do the placement outcomes match your career target — academic, industry, or home country?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If data is unavailable: A department that cannot or will not share placement data is a yellow flag — consider why that data isn't public

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your application list tiered — does it include programs where you have a realistic chance of admission, or is it concentrated at the top of the range?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies the prestige-only application strategy failure pattern before it results in zero admissions
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If tiered: Have you identified specific faculty matches and research fit justifications at each tier, not just ranked the schools?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If concentrated at top only: What is your plan if all top applications are rejected — another cycle, MS track, or reconfiguring the list now?

industry_realities.common_belief: Program rankings are a reliable proxy for career outcomes
industry_realities.actual_reality: Rankings measure research output and prestige metrics that predict academic job market success but not industry careers; within PhD programs, advisor relationship and research quality are more predictive than overall rank
industry_realities.implication: Students should research advisor placement records and alumni industry outcomes directly rather than defaulting to rankings as a shortcut

industry_realities.common_belief: A Masters degree from a top-brand university is a safe investment that will pay off
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many professional MS programs are revenue-generating tuition programs with no funding; total cost can exceed $200,000 for international students; employment outcomes are not guaranteed and OPT deadlines create time pressure
industry_realities.implication: International students must calculate actual ROI using real placement data and compare against the funded PhD alternative before committing

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD programs at top schools provide funding to all admitted students
industry_realities.actual_reality: Some PhD programs admit students without guaranteed funding, expecting them to find RA or TA positions after enrollment; funding can also disappear if the advisor loses grant support
industry_realities.implication: Students must verify the funding structure explicitly — whether stipend is guaranteed, for how many years, and at what institutional level — before accepting any offer

industry_realities.common_belief: Prestige transfers universally across career contexts
industry_realities.actual_reality: Rankings matter specifically for academic hiring pipelines, elite consulting/finance recruiting, and home-country brand recognition — they are largely irrelevant for most US industry employers who screen on skills and projects
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should map the specific career context they're targeting and determine whether rank is an actual screening filter in that context before weighting it heavily

industry_realities.common_belief: A well-known advisor with many students is a better mentor
industry_realities.actual_reality: Highly productive advisors with large labs often cannot give adequate individual mentorship — advising quality per student decreases as lab size increases
industry_realities.implication: Students should assess advisor-to-student ratio and meeting frequency directly, not infer mentorship quality from advisor prestige or publication count

industry_realities.common_belief: Program quality is uniform across the department
industry_realities.actual_reality: PhD experiences are highly advisor-specific — two students in the same top-10 department can have radically different outcomes based on their advisor's grant status, mentorship quality, and professional network
industry_realities.implication: Program-level evaluation is insufficient; students must evaluate the specific advisor relationship as the primary unit of analysis

industry_realities.common_belief: Location doesn't matter much — you can job search from anywhere
industry_realities.actual_reality: Programs near tech hubs have structurally richer recruiting pipelines, networking events, and internship access; international students on OPT face hard job search deadlines that make geographic disadvantage costly
industry_realities.implication: Location should be an explicit factor in program evaluation, especially for international students targeting US industry employment post-graduation

industry_realities.common_belief: A higher stipend always means a better financial situation
industry_realities.actual_reality: Cost of living varies dramatically — a $30,000 stipend in Pittsburgh is materially more livable than $30,000 in San Francisco or NYC; quality of life and savings rate over 5–6 years differ substantially
industry_realities.implication: Students should normalize stipend by cost of living index, not compare absolute dollar amounts across programs in different geographies

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Uses US News overall ranking as the primary decision input; assumes higher rank equals better outcome
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Evaluates advisor-specific placement records, subfield reputation, alumni outcomes in target career track, and funding security — ranks are a starting filter, not a decision
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Ranking-based decisions lead to mismatched advisor relationships and poor outcomes; advisor-based decisions drive actual career results

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes all PhD programs fully fund all students; does not distinguish between guaranteed multi-year funding and contingent annual funding
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Verifies funding structure explicitly — guaranteed vs. contingent, department-level vs. advisor-grant-dependent — before accepting any offer
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Contingent funding can collapse mid-program, leaving international students with no income, no visa support, and no clear path to graduation

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Defaults to MS as the 'safer' or 'faster' path without calculating total cost or comparing against funded PhD alternatives
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Calculates actual total cost of unfunded MS ($150,000–$200,000), compares against funded PhD net income and credential value, and makes an explicit ROI-informed decision
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The difference between choices can be $200,000 in cost and years of career trajectory — making this the highest-stakes financial decision in the application process

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Applies only to top-ranked programs because they are the most recognizable; no tiering for fit or admission probability
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Builds a tiered list with specific faculty matches at each tier; includes safety programs where admission is realistic; optimizes for the best achievable fit, not the highest brand name
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Prestige-only application strategies result in zero admissions when the profile doesn't match elite program expectations

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats the acceptance offer as sufficient information; may not visit, interview current students, or verify advisor availability
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Contacts current PhD students without the advisor present, asks about meeting frequency and mentorship quality, verifies active grants, and assesses lab culture before committing
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A 5–6 year life decision made on incomplete information risks discovering a toxic lab or disengaged advisor after enrollment, when switching is costly

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes prestige transfers universally — to industry, to home country, to every career context
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Maps prestige value to specific contexts where it is an actual screening filter (academic hiring, elite consulting/finance, home-country brand recognition) and deprioritizes it where it is not
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Over-weighting prestige in non-prestige-sensitive contexts leads to worse financial and career outcomes than choosing fit-matched programs

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Ignores geographic location or treats it as a lifestyle preference unrelated to career outcomes
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Explicitly evaluates program location relative to target employer geography, recruiting pipeline density, and OPT job search timeline constraints
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: For international students, geographic disadvantage during OPT can directly cause failed job searches — the deadline cannot be extended by working harder
